So far, I've at least understood that I need to build my identity from scratch, not one that relies on outside validation, and have a very good understanding of my wants and needs.', '[TITLE] My OCD Advice
[BODY] As someone who likely has had OCD/ADHD/Bipolar at the same time and has a college degree in Psychology + minor in neuroscience, here's what I suggest for the psychological aspect of it, regardless of what medications/therapy you might be on. 

1. "Thought crimes" do not exist. You have a basic human right to think about whatever you want at any time. Trying to suppress any unnatural/weird/"sinful" thoughts will not help and only catastrophically worsen obsessions and compulsions because those 2 are actually a defense mechanism to the initial distress of the thought. Trying to moderate random thoughts is a very unreasonable ask/standard for living beings. And it doesn't accomplish anything. No one will ever know or sense whatever you're thinking, whether it's genuine or not. So let thoughts flow, and don't fight them or analyze them, just go "whatever". They will pass naturally after that. There are no moral standards whatsoever to thoughts/urges. The fact that society has actually brainwashed people to think like this is shameful, and the main cause of unnecessary mental distress in life. Don't even put an ounce of effort into controlling that lol, if just the idea of something puts you in that much distress, you obviously are never going to do it in real life, so don't bother monitoring it..etc.

2. Many people say that the problem is never being able to satisfy or resist whatever compulsions they feel are needed to solve/prevent whatever problem/fear in their mind at the moment. So what you have to do is attack a different aspect of it. What you have to realize is that even if the terrible things you are imagining WERE rational, the distress you're experiencing 24/7365 fighting it is definitely WORSE than whatever imagined effect of the thing you're fighting on anyone else. Your suffering and catastrophic affect on your life is worse, undeserved, and unjustified for whatever moral standard you're trying to uphold for yourself. It's an unreasonable ask of anyone to expect you to go through that, even if the thing you're fearing was more rational. You aren't obligated to "prevent it". For example, let's say instead of germophobia, you feel excessively guilty about the risk of spreading germs. Maybe you are worried even 12+ days after you're sick that you're still contagious and do exaggerated measures to prevent spreading any leftover germs..etc. If this constantly interferes with your daily life, makes you incapacitated, makes you feel irrationally guilty all the time (or insert whatever fear in here), you have to say to yourself:

"What I'm going through is much worse suffering than the possible result of my not caring about preventing whatever harm I think might happen" and proceed to not care. 

So you're not fighting the obsessions/compulsions anymore, you're saying you don't care what the effect of not giving in to them (or giving in to them) anymore, so there's no REASON to WORRY about the compulsions anymore, because you're simple doing self-preservation by taking the easy way out. You aren't obligated to worry soo much about the potential harmful effects of XYZ (likely exaggerated/irrational anyway) if THIS is the cost of you doing it. Nope, you dont have to be a perfect human or even "above average morally" human. Your distress/incapacitation/misery is asking too much EVEN if the harmful effect was real. You're suffering more and that's unjusitifable.

So going back to the germs spreading thing, I said to myself "screw this I'm not going to struggle like this for the purpose of being flawlessly selfless, and just breathed coughed wherever I want (even deliberately as like a protest lol)". The odds are very low of anyone else getting sick after 12+ days of getting sick myself, and even if the 1% chance came true and someone else got it, I DON'T CARE! My struggling worrying about it constantly, whether rationally or not, is not worth that level of selflessness. You got to get angry about it and say "I am worth more than this and am under no obligation to be a saint and worry about how every little trivial action might affect other people". Fuck it. That's I how I recovered significantly when I went through things like this for a period a few years ago. This doesn't mean you're going to give in to every bizarre thought you have, it just means you aren't going to put that extra effort into being a perfect person, and even if that did indirectly negatively affect someone else..who cares? The negative effect on you is WORSE, so you can't be morally expected to worry about it! You don't have to do anything unreasonable, have to put yourself through unimaginable distress to "help other people" in your mind. That is how you conquer any irrational guilt aspects, that you don't owe anyone or society that Mother Teresa perfection in the first place. So now those compulsions and obsessions are not big deal because they are pointless. You don't have to keep fighting a futile battle because the end result is what doesn't matter, not the things themselves. 

3. Most OCD problems are caused by neurotransmitter imbalances, which can't just be willed away with cognitive behavior therapy or force of mind. Effective medication is what's needed. But it's important to note that not all SSRIs for example are designed for OCD. There are specific medications out there for this condition and not just generalized anxiety/depression (and even those 2 are actually inversely correlated, which is why SSRIs often randomly worsen symptoms occasionally). If a medication isn't designed to target OCD specifically, it may just end up enhancing your mental state of whatever you are feeling in the moment, good or bad (my personal experience with Lexapro at one point). So being prescribed the precise drug is essential, not just any one of a class of medications, if you decide on trying medication. And this point is extremely important. Popping a pill to relieve the distress is not weak or lame in the slightest. You have already lost so much time and happiness and productivity from this, you have EVERY RIGHT to take the easy way out. You shouldn't have to put an ounce of effort into curing yourself anymore. Like I said, you don't DESERVE that extra struggle. So if medication works, sit back and enjoy it, you aren't obligated to be the "better tough self-reliant independent human", you don't have anything to prove. It's a stupid neurotransmitter imbalance, that's it! So ignore people who say things like "I never needed a mental health pill"..etc, you have the human rights to not suffer to such extent. You are ENTITLED to the easier way out lol!']

['[TITLE] Just found out I am OCPD, not Asperger’s
[BODY] So, plot twist: after spending 2 months convinced and years of suspicion I was on Team Asperger, turns out I’m officially diagnosed with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder instead.

I want to apologize to everyone for posting as if I was Asperger’s. I was truly convinced I was and found huge resemblance and relief interacting with each and everyone of you. Now that my psychologist explained to me my condition and why I can’t be Asperger, I can’t stop feeling like a fraud and I offer my most sincere apologies to the [SUBREDDIT] community. 

The process of figuring out about my true nature has been cathartic and it couldn’t have been possible if I hadn’t taking the route of self diagnosing me as Asperger’s. There are many traits that overlap with both mental disorders and my psychologist told me it’s worth working on them (Asperger’s traits) as well. 

The reasoning why I can’t be Asperger’s is because she concluded I was better at masking during my childhood and adolescence and I got worse in my adulthood. From her experience, most Aspies improve their masking skills over time. Additionally she noted high level of structure, control and perfectionism in my personality. 

I guess convincing myself I am Asperger’s after watching hundreds of hours of YouTube, reading books and scientific literature in record time … is kinda OCPD. 

I want to thank to all the people who shared their experiences and genuine advice. I couldn’t have reached to this understanding level of myself without all of you!', "[TITLE] Bring back the term “Asperger’s” to the DSM
[BODY] I understand why the term “Asperger’s” was removed from the DSM, largely due to Hans Asperger’s problematic history and to simplify the autism spectrum. But I believe removing it entirely may have had unintended consequences for those it previously described. Here’s why:

1. Loss of Identity: Many people strongly identified with “Asperger’s” as a distinct part of their experience. It described a specific set of traits, and removing it left some feeling like their identity was erased or that they no longer fit into a clear category.
2. Spectrum Confusion: The autism spectrum is incredibly broad, from individuals who need full-time support to those who are independent but experience social and sensory challenges. The Asperger’s label helped differentiate between these experiences, creating clearer understanding both for those on the spectrum and those trying to support them.
3. Missed Understanding of Unique Strengths: “Asperger’s” highlighted strengths in logical thinking, focus, and specific interests, helping people see that there were positives to their neurodivergence. Without this label, some may not have the same sense of the unique positives associated with Asperger’s.
4. Medical and Social Support: The lack of this distinct diagnosis can sometimes make it harder for people to get tailored support or accommodations that suit their needs, as their specific challenges may be overlooked within the broader autism spectrum.
5. Tolerance: Many people seem to tolerate the term “Asperger’s” more easily than “autism.” “Asperger’s” often feels less stigmatized, carrying a milder or more familiar connotation for some. As a result, when someone identifies as having Asperger’s, others might not “freak out” as much or react as strongly as they would to the term “autism.” This difference in reaction can make it easier for those diagnosed to find acceptance and understanding from others, even if the challenges they face are part of the broader autism spectrum.

Perhaps we can't bring Asperger's back, but we can make Autism Spectrum Profile for Individual Expression (ASPIE) become an official term /s", '[TITLE] Question about Asperger’s
[BODY] Why do neurotypicals seem to delight in criticising people with autis?']

['[TITLE] Do y’all ever close an app just to reopen it again in less than 2 seconds?

I should check [the app i just had open]”. And then I open the app again and realize that I JUST had it open, and I feel incredibly… stupid.', '[TITLE] I quit social media over the span of 6 months. Here's how it went.
[BODY] I used to be one of those people who couldn't stay off social media. I needed constant stimulation and couldn't cope with periods of "boredom". Just last year, I was averaging about 7 hours of screen time every day. And I thought nothing of it. 

But then I noticed that my work was slipping. My coworkers were always annoyed with me because I was too addicted to my phone. There were times where I genuinely didn't want to come to work because I wanted to spend all day online. They often had to pick up my slack, which made them resent working with me. Back then, I was so frustrated with my job that I didn't really care how my phone addiction was affecting others. But when I realized it was affecting my relationships, I knew I needed to change. 

Slowly, I started getting rid of my social media accounts. I think I started with Tumblr first. It was easy to get rid of because it was just endless scrolling through aesthetic photos and annoying hot takes. Once I got rid of Tumblr, I noticed that I stopped being so hyperfixated on other people's opinions. I used to be so afraid of being seen as problematic, and that fear has completely disappeared.

Next was Facebook. That one was kinda difficult, because I used to use it for things like Buy Nothing groups in my area. It was also one of the few ways that I could keep track of my family. I remember spending so much time just scrolling through my feed and looking at memes and other people's day to day lives. I realized I was spending too much time engrossed in everyone else that I was neglecting myself. I made the tough decision to back up all my photos and delete my account. Since then, I've been more focused on myself and my own needs. 

The biggest struggle I've had was getting rid of Tiktok. I don't know what it is about short form media that's so addictive, but it was by far the hardest to give up. For some reason, I always considered Tiktok to be a valuable source of information. I used to get my news from Tiktok and would use it to look up tutorials and other things I needed to research. But that's the problem with Tiktok: it's not a credible source. I was pretty hypocritical, calling out people for not having credible sources when I was primarily using Tiktok for my arguments. 

Getting a new phone is what helped me quit Tiktok cold turkey. I was able to just install the bare minimum apps that I needed to function. I also installed a minimalist launcher to keep the temptations low. Reddit is really the only social platform I use now.

Overall, I've noticed that my mental health has significantly improved. I'm no longer doomscrolling and I'm a lot more present. Ironically, quitting social media has made me a lot more social. I never used to engage in small talk, but now I've found myself chatting up strangers when I'm out. Outside of having to use my phone for work, my screen time has dropped significantly. That's given me time to really explore the city I live in and start doing the things I love doing again. For the first time in years, I was able to pick up a book and focus on reading again!!

I apologize for this post being so long, I just wanted to share my story. I'm very proud of myself for how far I've come!', "[TITLE] I can't believe how much time I was wasting on tiktok and reels in general

['[TITLE] Do you grind or clench your teeth during sleep?
[BODY] Any relation to ptsd? How do you feel when you wake up?', '[TITLE] I got my teeth fixed after years of not brushing due to my depression.
[BODY] Hi. I’m 19(F) and I’ve been working on getting my teeth fixed after years of neglecting to brush my teeth due to my depression. I’ve struggled with depression for many years now, since I was 13/14 and the last couple of years have been the hardest years of my life. One of the most difficult parts of it was struggling to take care of myself and my daily hygiene, showering, and brushing my teeth. I always felt so drained and could never get myself to get the energy to go take a shower and brush my teeth. Brushing my teeth was more difficult for me though.

Obviously, over time my teeth started to get really bad, and had cavities on all my front teeth. I became very self-conscious because of my teeth and smiling was one of my biggest insecurities. but the last year or so, I finally decided I wanted to try and improve myself and push myself to take care of my teeth and get myself to a dentist. I was also getting some pain whenever I would eat certain foods and it was painful whenever I did try to brush. So I really had to do something before it got even worse. 

Since then I’ve been working on taking care of myself better and I’ve been doing a lot better with brushing my teeth every day. The dentist I’ve been going to has been incredible, very kind, and understanding, and helped me feel comfortable through each appointment I’ve had along with giving me the laughing gas which helped too. At first, I was terrified of going and terrified I’d waited too long and lost my teeth but thankfully I didn’t. 

Around September of 2023, I had my first appointment to get my teeth looked at along with some X-rays, and then have two deep clean appointments for each side of my mouth. I spent time with my family in another state for a few months and began my filling appointments when I got back. Since late March I’ve been doing a lot of filling appointments. They started with some smaller cavities in the back and for the last couple of weeks they’ve been working on my front teeth and just had my final filling appointment for my front teeth a few days ago. My teeth are finally fixed!

My teeth have been looking so much better now and have improved so much. I only have a few more appointments and I’m finally done! I have to get a back tooth removed and a small cavity in the very back filled and then after that I’m done for a while. They did say that I’ll need root canals and crowns sometime in the future but thankfully not right now. But after so many years of struggling and months of dental work, I’ve finally gotten my smile back and this is the most I’ve ever felt proud of myself. 

I’ve also been doing so much better with brushing my teeth and flossing every day. While I’m working on it, I’m also doing better with showering more often as well. While I still often feel drained and feel like I have no energy I still try to push myself hard to take care of myself better and keep up with my daily hygiene. And now that my smile is back maybe this is a sign I’m starting to heal and begin recovering from my depression. While my depression still often lingers and comes in waves I hope to get to recovery someday. I often wonder if It will ever go away for me but I hope for it someday.', '[TITLE] Issues with brushing teeth
[BODY] Does anyone else have issues brushing their teeth daily? I have no problem showering, brushing my hair, deodorant, clean clothes. Everything but brushing my teeth. Has anyone have that issue and how did you get passed it?']

['[TITLE] It sucks to feel nervous and not know what to do in a conversation — I want to change that
[BODY] I recently realized that I really need to improve my communication skills. I get very nervous when I have to talk to people — I get flustered, say things without thinking, or lose my train of thought and end up confused in the middle of a conversation.

For a long time, I thought my communication was “okay,” but now I see I’ve always been in my comfort zone: my childhood friends. I have one friend group in real life and two online, but I made all three groups when I was a kid — I don’t even remember how I managed to become friends with them. It just happened naturally, I guess.

I’ve tried a few times to make new friends online, but I failed because I just can’t keep up with talking daily. Some people left and new ones joined, but I never went out of my way to find new people to talk to.

About two years ago, something happened that made me lose my confidence in speaking to people. I became more withdrawn and scared of talking. I think I’ve recovered a lot since then, but I still feel the fear. For example, I was never able to present school projects because I was too shy. But recently, for the first time ever, I actually did it twice! It wasn’t perfect, but it felt good to face that fear after so many years of running away.

Still, I notice that I can only talk to strangers on the street if I’m with a friend. Alone, I freeze. I’ve tried to push myself, but it’s really hard. For example, I tried going on Omegle to talk to random people — but the first person that appeared made me so nervous that my heart raced and my body felt hot, so I left immediately and never went back.I also tried VRChat because I thought it might be easier, but that didn’t work either. One time, I was in a map and saw three people standing a bit apart — I walked over to them to try to start a conversation, but for some reason I got so nervous that I couldn’t say anything. I left without saying a word, even though I really wanted to talk. Other times I tried speaking to groups, but it felt like no one could hear me. They seemed like nice people, but I had no idea how to get closer to them — even though I wanted to talk, I could only stand there listening.

I really don’t like this. I wish I could make more friends and not get so nervous in these situations. Even simple things become awkward: today I went to the doctor and he reached out his hand to take a paper from me, but I thought he was greeting me — so I shook his hand and then handed over the paper. It was funny, but it shows how my insecurity makes me act without thinking.

Sometimes I see people on the street who look attractive or interesting, and I wish I could just say something, but I freeze. I keep thinking, “What should I say?” “What if they ignore me?” “What if I don’t know what to say next?” Recently, I saw someone really beautiful who looked like an old crush I hadn’t seen in years — but I couldn’t say anything. I felt pathetic about that.

With my friends, I talk a lot — even when I don’t know what to say, I still feel free to be myself. But with strangers, it’s like I forget how to talk at all.

Is the only way to get better at this really just to practice? To push myself to talk to more people? It’s so hard and honestly so scary for me. I want to be able to strike up conversations, make new friends, or just say something silly to strangers when I feel like it.

If anyone here has gone through something similar or has any advice, I’d love to hear it. Thank you so much for reading all of this.', '[TITLE] How to get over my voice insecurities
[BODY] My entire life I've been bullied for my voice. I have a speech impediment due to my autism. Back in elementary school, kids would constantly accuse me of having my "own language" and therefore "not understand me." They'd sneer and giggle. Growing up this has faded, but I can tell the hate still lays there

People, including my friends have mocked my studder while angry/upset with me. I am often corrected of how to say a word and people will laugh when I say a word incorrectly. They don't mean any harm, but it still hurts. Because now whenever I listen to recordings of my voice all I hear is a little kid. My voice has a weird tone to it and just...doesn't sound right. It sounds childish

How do I overcome this? I've done as much speech therapy as I can', '[TITLE] weird voice

Name: 17_apps_journaling_productivity_tracking
Representative_Docs:
['[TITLE] This worked for me, maybe it will work for you
[BODY] Dear Reader 

This post is going to be an attempt to communicate to you a lot of the things I have learnt in the past 3 months.

I am going to try to teach you what I have learned about Journaling, keeping a consistent practice, enjoying the process, and, in general, how to not get yourself all screwed up trying to find the "optimal" way to journal.

Anyway, let's get started. As you know, Journaling can be extremely beneficial to your overall well-being and, strange as it may seem, it's also one of the hardest things to do consistently.

You know what? I've been trying to "start" journaling for the past 10 years, it's like meditation, you know that it's good for you, but damn it is hard to do consistently. 

 
Well, anyway, this all leads me to the first and most important thing I want to write about which is not being too strict in HOW you Journal. In my opinion, it's the number one reason why people never get started and, if they do, they most likely don't stick to it. In fact, in my opinion, the best way to get into the mood to Journal is to Journal, but, but how? Well that's what we are going to cover here.

Before we know what to do, let's look at what not to do.

How To Mess Up:

- Overthink Paper vs Digital for as long as you can 
- Buy the most expensive Journal you can find (extra credit: Get a feather Quil and learn cursive). 
- Spend hours, days or weeks to find the ideal first Journal entry. 
- Comb the internet to find the best way to Journal, read every post you find and, then, do nothing.

Listen guys, I've done all of this (okay, not the Quil thing, but the rest).

 
What I did:

Here are some tips. First of all, I suggest you do not spend hours researching how to Journal and just start, In other words, just pick up a pen and a piece of paper and write. 

Now, if that seems too difficult, welcome to the club.

I felt that Journaling into the void was not for me, I wanted feedback on my writing, and I wanted it from someone who I looked up to. So, I procrastinated and build built my own Journal App that uses Historical figures to give me feedback and ask questions about my writing.

But, here's the thing, it worked. Having Carl Jung or Marcus Aurelius (two people who I admire) give me feedback on my writing, ask me questions and, relate it back to their own lives, worked, for me. 

Since then I've given it to people I know that Journal (or try to Journal) and they really enjoy using it.

So I'm posting here to see if there is anyone in this group who would like to try it out? 

I really hope you get started journaling, it's helped me more than I could ever imagine.', '[TITLE] What ADHD Apps do you use?
[BODY] Hey ADHDers!👋

I’ve been on a journey to find the best apps to help with productivity, time management, and staying on top of things. As someone with ADHD, I know how tricky it can be to find the right tools that actually work for our unique brains.

I’m curious—what apps are you all using at the moment to help with these challenges? Whether it’s a to-do list, calendar, or something more specialized, I’d love to hear what works for you.

Also, are there any features you wish these apps had? Maybe something that could make them even more ADHD-friendly?

Thanks in advance for your suggestions!

[Edit] Wow, thank you all for the amazing responses! I didn’t expect this post to get so much attention. I hope it becomes a helpful resource for anyone with ADHD searching for solutions—it’s certainly been eye-opening for me. From what I’ve gathered, there are a lot of great options out there, but it’s important to find what works best for you since everyone’s needs are different. Thank You all ❤️', '[TITLE] How Journaling Completely Transformed My Life (And It Can Change Yours Too)
[BODY] I started journaling about a year ago, and it has completely transformed my life. If you’ve been thinking about giving it a shot, here’s why you should:

I used to struggle with overthinking, feeling stuck in life, and lacking clarity about my goals. My mind was constantly racing, replaying conversations or worrying about things outside my control. Journaling wasn’t something I ever saw myself doing—it felt too cliché, too much like writing in a diary as a kid. But one day, feeling overwhelmed, I decided to give it a try.

Fast forward to now, and here’s what I’ve noticed:

 • Clarity in decision-making: Writing down my thoughts forced me to confront and organize them. I started seeing patterns and finding answers I didn’t realize were already in my mind.

 • Improved mental health: By putting my emotions on paper, I gave them a place to exist outside my head. This made my worries feel less overwhelming.

 • Better problem-solving: Journaling helped me break down complex issues into manageable pieces, leading to actionable solutions.

 • Stronger sense of gratitude: Writing about what went well each day made me appreciate the little things and helped me shift my focus away from negativity.

 • Progress tracking: I could actually see how far I’d come by revisiting old entries. It motivated me to keep going.

 • A more positive mindset: When I journaled about struggles, I often found myself naturally writing about possible solutions, which helped me approach problems with a proactive attitude.

 • Increased productivity: By setting daily intentions in my journal, I stayed focused and achieved more in less time.

 • Better self-awareness: Journaling gave me insights into my triggers, strengths, and areas for growth.

How I got started:
 1. Keep it simple: I started with just 5-10 minutes a day, often writing about what I was feeling or what happened that day. No rules, no pressure.

 2. Prompt yourself: On days when I didn’t know what to write, I’d answer questions like, “What went well today?” or “What’s one thing I’m worried about, and why?”

 3. Be honest: The journal is for you. There’s no need to sugarcoat anything—write what you really feel.

 4. Experiment: I tried different styles—stream-of-consciousness, gratitude lists, bullet journaling—and stuck with what resonated.

 5. Be consistent: Even on busy days, I’d write one sentence. It was more about the habit than the content.

 6. Don’t judge your writing: The goal isn’t to create art—it’s to express yourself.

Some days I still feel stuck, but journaling has become a tool I rely on to process emotions, solve problems, and stay grounded. If you’ve been hesitant, I encourage you to give it a try. A notebook and a pen might just change your life, too.

Good luck!']
